title: OS Credential Dumping
summary: OS Credential Dumping is the parent behaviour of extracting account secrets from an operating system, usually as password hashes or clear text passwords. The material lives in different places depending on platform: process memory such as LSASS on Windows, registry hives holding the Security Account Manager or LSA secrets, the Active Directory database on domain controllers, caches built for offline logon, and files such as the Linux shadow file. The adversary normally needs administrative or SYSTEM rights, and the payoff is a reusable secret that supports lateral movement and access to restricted information. Detections combine process access telemetry, command line history, creation of dump artefacts, and abnormal reads of sensitive registry or disk locations. Legitimate backup, troubleshooting and endpoint security products touch the same sources, so context such as the calling process, its parent, its signature and the timing decides whether an event is malicious.

beginner.definition: An operating system keeps account secrets so that users can log in quickly. Credential dumping means stealing those secrets. Attackers copy them out of memory, files or the registry. The stolen secrets can then be used to log in as other users.
beginner.whyItMatters: One stolen secret can give an attacker access to many systems. Password hashes can often be reused without knowing the real password. This turns a single infected computer into a path across the whole network. If you do not watch for it, the first sign may be a serious breach. Knowing the sources helps you protect and monitor the right places.
howItWorks: An attacker gains high level rights, such as administrator or SYSTEM, on a machine.
They choose a source of secrets, such as memory, a registry hive or a file.
A tool copies that data into a file or sends it to another machine.
The copy is processed offline to recover passwords or usable hashes.
The recovered secrets are reused to log in to other systems.
Defenders may see only a normal administration tool reading a sensitive location.
beginner.example: Think of a hospital night desk that keeps a drawer of master keys. A thief cannot open patient rooms, so instead they copy the master keys and walk away. Nothing in the building looks broken and no door was forced. Later, the copies open many rooms quietly. Credential dumping works the same way. The attacker copies the keys to the whole building instead of breaking one lock.
takeaways: Credential dumping steals reusable secrets, not just one user password.
Legitimate administration and backup tools touch the same data sources.
Context, not a single event, tells you whether the access was malicious.

objectives: Explain what OS credential dumping is and why stolen secrets are reusable.
List the Windows and Linux locations where credential material is stored.
Describe the level of access an adversary normally needs for this technique.
Explain how dumped secrets support lateral movement across a network.
Identify telemetry that reveals unusual access to credential stores.
